paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of finding analytical Lyapunov functions for nonlinear dynamical systems. Existing approaches that represent these functions with neural networks can be difficult to interpret and formally verify. The authors instead generate symbolic mathematical expressions, making the resulting candidates more accessible to control engineers and better suited to formal checking.

Their framework pairs a transformer that proposes expressions with a falsifier that checks candidates during training. Feedback from these checks improves the generator through a risk-seeking policy-gradient method. Training starts from scratch using reinforcement learning. Efficient optimization methods support falsification during learning, while separate formal verification tools check the final expressions.

The reported experiments cover nonlinear systems with up to ten dimensions, including non-polynomial systems. The method finds local Lyapunov functions, so its demonstrated scope concerns local rather than global behavior. The authors also report discovering functions not previously identified in the control literature. Together, these findings support symbolic generation as a route toward interpretable, verifiable results for challenging dynamical systems.
icml-2025-analytical-lyapunov-function-d.tldr: A reinforcement-learning transformer generates symbolic local Lyapunov functions that can be formally verified for nonlinear systems with up to ten dimensions.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial resources communicating gradients between workers. Compressing those gradients reduces communication, but the choice of compressor creates a trade-off. Biased compressors can work well empirically, while unbiased compressors offer statistical properties that support theoretical guarantees. The paper seeks to combine these advantages within a single compression framework.

The proposed approach uses Multilevel Monte Carlo to construct statistically unbiased estimates from biased compressors. The crucial distinction is between the compression operations used as ingredients and the estimate produced by the overall scheme: biased ingredients can contribute to an unbiased final estimate. This gives the framework a way to retain useful compression methods while addressing their bias.

The authors apply the scheme to Top-k and bit-wise compressors and also derive an adaptive version intended to improve performance further. They evaluate the approach on distributed deep learning tasks. Its stated contribution is therefore both a general construction and implementations for familiar compression choices, with empirical validation supporting its use beyond the statistical formulation.
icml-2025-beyond-communication-overhead-.tldr: A Multilevel Monte Carlo scheme turns biased gradient compressors into statistically unbiased estimators for distributed learning.

paragraphs: WASP addresses synthetic training-data generation when only a small amount of private data is available. The goal is to produce useful samples resembling that private data within a differential-privacy setting. Limited examples make this difficult because the generator must contend with an uncertain picture of the desired data, generation noise, and biases already present in pretrained models.

The framework combines two mechanisms. A Top-Q voting procedure uses the available private samples to estimate their distribution more accurately. A contrastive generation process then uses low-quality synthetic samples as informative material, while multiple pretrained generative models collaborate with dynamically adjusted weights. This makes both model diversity and unsuccessful synthetic examples part of the generation strategy.

The authors evaluate WASP on six datasets using six open-source and three closed-source pretrained models. They report improved model performance across varied downstream tasks. These findings support the usefulness of combining private-data estimation with weighted multi-model generation, particularly for the data-deficient setting that motivates the method.
icml-2025-contrastive-private-data-synth.tldr: WASP combines private-data voting, contrastive generation, and dynamically weighted pretrained models to improve synthetic training data when private examples are scarce.

paragraphs: EasyRef aims to make diffusion models use the visual elements shared across several reference images. Simply averaging or concatenating independently encoded images does not let the references interact to identify what they have in common. Methods that learn from each image group can capture these elements, but require additional fine-tuning for every new group.

The proposed method uses a multimodal language model to examine the references together and follow instructions about which consistent elements matter, such as visual style or facial identity. Adapters transfer its representations into the diffusion process. An efficient reference-aggregation strategy and progressive training scheme are designed to reduce computation while preserving fine details.

The paper also introduces MRBench for evaluating generation from multiple reference images. Experiments report that EasyRef outperforms both tuning-free and tuning-based alternatives, with stronger aesthetic quality and zero-shot generalization across diverse domains. The central result is that instruction-guided understanding of an image group can provide useful conditioning for generation without requiring separate test-time fine-tuning for each group.
icml-2025-easyref-omni-generalized-group.tldr: EasyRef uses a multimodal language model to extract instruction-selected visual elements shared across reference images and guide diffusion generation.

paragraphs: FRUGAL targets the memory consumed by optimizer state during large language model training. Existing memory-saving approaches can restrict the effective rank of weight updates, potentially discarding important gradient information. The authors highlight this concern especially for pretraining, where losing update directions can undermine the benefit of reducing memory use.

The framework splits the gradient into two parts. A low-dimensional part receives updates from an optimizer such as Adam, while the remaining directions receive updates from state-free methods such as SGD or signSGD. This preserves full-rank updates without storing expensive optimizer state for every direction. The splitting framework can work with selection techniques used by GaLore and BAdam.

The theoretical convergence result applies specifically to a combination of momentum SGD for low-dimensional updates and SGD for the other directions. Empirically, the authors report consistent improvements over concurrent approaches and state-of-the-art results on pretraining and fine-tuning tasks. The contribution is a way to balance memory and training performance by varying the optimizer across directions while continuing to update all of them.
icml-2025-frugal-memory-efficient-optimi.tldr: FRUGAL saves optimizer memory by using stateful optimization in selected directions and state-free updates elsewhere, preserving full-rank weight updates.

paragraphs: Hard Preference Sampling addresses how language models learn to favor human-preferred answers and reject undesirable ones. The authors identify weaknesses in existing preference methods, including inefficient use of rejected responses, difficulty handling harmful content, and high computation for methods based on the Plackett-Luce model. HPS changes both the training objective and how training examples are sampled.

Its loss prioritizes the most preferred response while pushing against all dispreferred and harmful responses. Particular emphasis goes to hard dispreferred answers: responses that closely resemble preferred ones and therefore require a sharper distinction. A single-sample Monte Carlo strategy reduces computational overhead while maintaining alignment quality.

The theoretical analysis establishes improved sample efficiency over existing Plackett-Luce methods and maximization of the reward margin between preferred and dispreferred answers. Experiments on HH-RLHF and PKU-Safety report comparable BLEU and reward scores alongside substantially better reward margins and reduced harmful generation. The findings suggest that learning clearer preference boundaries can improve rejection behavior without sacrificing the reported measures of response quality.
icml-2025-hps-hard-preference-sampling-f.tldr: HPS emphasizes difficult rejected responses to improve preference separation and reduce harmful generation with lower sampling overhead.

paragraphs: MemVR addresses hallucinations in multimodal language models by revisiting visual information during answer generation. The authors connect these errors to how the text decoder responds to visual tokens: a model can behave as though it has forgotten information from the image. This motivates a mechanism that supplies the visual evidence again when it is needed.

During inference, high uncertainty triggers the reintroduction of visual tokens at an intermediate layer. These tokens enter through a feed-forward network as key-value memory, giving the model supplementary evidence while it generates its answer. The intervention is therefore tied to uncertainty during decoding, rather than treating the initial presentation of the image as sufficient for every later prediction.

Across evaluations involving several multimodal models, the authors report significant hallucination reductions and strong performance on general benchmarks without additional time overhead. The findings support repeated access to visual representations as a practical way to improve factual alignment. They establish mitigation in the evaluated settings, rather than elimination of every possible hallucination.
icml-2025-look-twice-before-you-answer-m.tldr: MemVR reinjects visual evidence when a multimodal model becomes uncertain during decoding, reducing hallucinations without reported additional time overhead.

paragraphs: MedXpertQA is a benchmark designed to test demanding medical knowledge and advanced reasoning. It contains 4,460 questions covering 17 specialties and 11 body systems, organized into text-only and multimodal subsets. Its purpose is to provide a more challenging and clinically relevant evaluation than existing benchmarks whose questions may be insufficiently difficult.

The multimodal subset combines expert-level exam questions with varied images and substantial clinical context, including patient records and examination results. This gives the evaluation richer material than simple question-answer pairs derived from image captions. The construction process also uses filtering, augmentation, specialty board questions, data synthesis to reduce leakage risk, and repeated expert review.

The authors evaluate 18 leading models and create a reasoning-oriented subset for assessing models with capabilities like those targeted by o1. Their broader motivation is that medicine provides a setting for reasoning connected to real-world decisions, extending evaluation beyond mathematics and programming. The contribution is the benchmark and its evaluation design; the supplied abstract does not identify a winning model.
icml-2025-medxpertqa-benchmarking-expert.tldr: MedXpertQA provides 4,460 expert-level medical questions, including rich multimodal cases, to evaluate knowledge and advanced reasoning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents that use world models can perform poorly when the environment changes suddenly. The changes considered here include altered visual properties and altered rules for how states evolve. A model learned under earlier conditions may no longer describe the environment accurately, creating a need to detect novelty during deployment.

The paper uses disagreement between the world model's imagined states and the states actually observed by the agent as a novelty score. In this context, hallucinated states are the model's generated predictions. The proposed bounding approaches turn their misalignment with observations into a way to detect changes relative to the transition distribution the agent has learned.

The authors report effective novelty detection and an advantage in a novel environment over both traditional machine-learning detection methods and established reinforcement-learning approaches. The key idea is to draw detection evidence from predictions the world model already supplies. This connects novelty detection directly to whether the agent's learned account of the environment continues to match its experience.
icml-2025-novelty-detection-in-reinforce.tldr: The method detects environmental novelty by measuring disagreement between a reinforcement-learning world model's predictions and observed states.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that compositional sparsity is central to explaining deep learning's success in high-dimensional problems. A function can depend on many inputs overall while being assembled from smaller constituent functions, each using only a few inputs. The authors propose that deep networks succeed by exploiting this structure in their targets.

The argument connects that structure to efficient computation. The authors show that efficiently Turing-computable functions share the relevant property and argue that it is therefore highly likely to occur in current learning problems. This offers a reason to study structured function families when explaining how deep networks cope with settings that challenge classical shallow networks.

The paper also separates existing theoretical progress from unresolved questions. Approximation and generalization already have promising results for compositionally sparse functions, but learnability and optimization remain incompletely understood. Its position is that a comprehensive theory needs to explain both the usefulness of this structure and how training discovers or exploits it, rather than treating representational advantages as a complete account of learning.
icml-2025-position-a-theory-of-deep-lear.tldr: The authors argue that deep-learning theory must explain how networks exploit functions built from low-dimensional components.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes a more collaborative role for language models in mental health care, with human expertise remaining central. The authors see potential benefits for access, personalization, and crisis intervention. They also identify barriers involving bias, evaluation, excessive reliance, dehumanization, and regulatory uncertainty, which motivate a structured approach to deployment.

The first proposed pathway, SAFE-i, organizes responsible implementation around supportive, adaptive, fair, and ethical principles. It covers data governance, model engineering, and integration into real-world care. The second, HAAS-e, focuses on human-centered assessment, broadening evaluation beyond technical accuracy to include trustworthiness, empathy, cultural sensitivity, and whether outputs support useful action.

These pathways address complementary questions: how a system should be built and introduced, and how its behavior should be judged. The paper advocates their adoption as a basis for responsible, scalable mental health support. Its contribution is a proposed implementation and evaluation agenda, with language models envisioned as collaborators that complement human professionals rather than replacing their expertise.
icml-2025-position-beyond-assistance-rei.tldr: The paper proposes paired implementation and evaluation frameworks for language models that collaborate responsibly with mental health professionals.

paragraphs: This position paper examines the gap between certified robustness research and practical security for AI systems. Certification is often presented as a solution to adversarial examples, but the authors argue that substantial obstacles remain before it can serve that role in real applications. Their concern is how technical guarantees translate into decisions and expectations during deployment.

The paper identifies three central gaps: a paradox described as detection without distinction, insufficient criteria for practitioners comparing certification schemes, and security risks created by expectations surrounding guaranteed robustness. Together, these issues concern the usefulness of a certification result and whether people understand what confidence they should place in it.

The authors call for concrete changes within the certification research community to make the field more practically applicable. The position does not dismiss the value of certification; it argues that meaningful deployment requires resolving these gaps. Its central implication is that a robustness claim and an assessment of model security cannot yet be treated as interchangeable outcomes.
icml-2025-position-certified-robustness-.tldr: The paper argues that certified robustness still faces practical and interpretive gaps before it can support real-world model security.

paragraphs: Theoretical reinforcement-learning research often judges algorithms by whether their regret bounds match lower bounds up to constant factors and sometimes logarithmic terms. This paper questions how much practical similarity that criterion establishes. The authors argue that multiplicative constants matter for actual performance and that algorithm design should at least reduce unnecessary exploration.

They develop the argument through finite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes. Starting from UCBVI, they improve its exploration bonus terms and the associated regret analysis. This makes the position constructive: the paper changes a specific algorithm and examines how refinements to the constants affect its behavior, instead of only criticizing the prevailing evaluation standard.

The empirical comparison includes the revised UCBVI, its original version, and the state-of-the-art MVP algorithm. The authors report significant performance benefits from improving multiplicative constants. These findings motivate closer attention to constants when comparing theoretical guarantees and suggest a concrete way to reduce the disconnect between what theoretical analyses emphasize and what practitioners experience.
icml-2025-position-constants-are-critica.tldr: An improved UCBVI analysis and algorithm show that reducing constants in regret bounds can substantially improve empirical reinforcement-learning performance.

paragraphs: This position paper examines licensing problems created by widespread publication and reuse of machine-learning models. Developers choose among licenses such as Apache-2.0, OpenRAIL, Creative Commons, Llama2, and GPL-3.0, but the authors identify a lack of accepted standards or best practices for model licensing. They argue that this fragmented situation creates risks of legal noncompliance.

The paper reviews clauses in commonly used licenses, compares their differences, and investigates current licensing practices. It then uses examples from real repositories on Hugging Face to illustrate potential legal risks. This connects the argument about inconsistent practices to concrete model-sharing settings, rather than treating the choice of license as an isolated administrative decision.

The authors also propose ModelGo Licenses, a new draft intended to address the identified challenges and improve compliance. The contribution combines a review of existing approaches with a proposed route toward standardization. Its stated concern is that continued model reuse without clearer licensing practices can carry legal risks, while a more coherent framework could help developers govern that reuse.
icml-2025-position-current-model-licensi.tldr: The authors identify compliance risks in fragmented model licensing and propose draft ModelGo Licenses as a route toward clearer practices.

paragraphs: This paper argues that small language-model benchmarks need different statistical treatment from large ones. Error bars and significance tests are essential for interpreting performance, but commonly used procedures rely on the Central Limit Theorem. The authors consider those methods appropriate for benchmarks containing thousands of examples while questioning their reliability on smaller, specialized evaluations.

In the small-data settings they examine, CLT-based procedures perform poorly and usually underestimate uncertainty substantially. The resulting error bars are too narrow, making an evaluation appear more precise than the evidence supports. The issue therefore affects how confidently a score or apparent performance difference can be interpreted, even when uncertainty measures are reported.

The paper recommends alternative frequentist and Bayesian methods described as easy to implement and more suitable for these settings. Its practical message is to match uncertainty estimation to the amount of evaluation data available. The warning is especially relevant as specialized benchmarks become more common: adding error bars is useful only when the statistical method gives an adequate account of uncertainty.
icml-2025-position-dont-use-the-clt-in-l.tldr: The authors show that CLT-based error bars often severely understate uncertainty on small LLM benchmarks and recommend alternative statistical methods.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that debates over generative-AI regulation can benefit from experience with social media. The authors begin by comparing what the two technologies enable and where they differ. Allegations of political bias provide one example of a recurring issue, suggesting that some regulatory questions already have relevant evidence and institutional experience.

The paper develops four recommendations from that comparison. It calls for addressing bias and perceptions of bias through measures such as transparency, oversight, researcher access, and democratic participation. It also recommends focusing on concrete concerns, including youth wellbeing and election integrity, while investing in trust and safety. The remaining recommendations emphasize computational social science research and a more global perspective.

The proposed value of this approach is to save effort and avoid preventable mistakes by learning from earlier regulatory developments. Because the argument explicitly considers differences as well as similarities, it supports informed adaptation of lessons rather than assuming the technologies are identical. The contribution is a policy agenda grounded in that comparison.
icml-2025-position-generative-ai-regulat.tldr: The paper draws four generative-AI policy recommendations from social media regulation, emphasizing bias, concrete harms, research, and global perspectives.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that graph-learning benchmarks are steering research away from broader practical impact. Although graph methods have shown promise in drug design and molecular prediction, the authors criticize an emphasis on narrow settings such as two-dimensional molecular graphs. They identify combinatorial optimization, databases, and chip design as areas deserving greater attention.

The critique also concerns what datasets represent and how results are compared. Poor abstractions can fail to capture the underlying data or fit the intended application. Fragmented evaluations and excessive emphasis on accuracy can then reward overfitting instead of producing insights that generalize. The authors connect these problems to the lack of truly useful graph foundation models.

Their proposed response is to build more meaningful benchmarks, use rigorous evaluation protocols, and collaborate more closely with domain experts. The argument treats benchmark design as a research priority because it determines which problems and successes receive attention. The paper's warning is that graph learning's continued relevance depends partly on whether its evaluations better reflect consequential applications.
icml-2025-position-graph-learning-will-l.tldr: The authors argue that narrow, poorly aligned benchmarks threaten graph learning's relevance and call for evaluations grounded in meaningful applications.

paragraphs: This position paper considers whether language models can simulate human research subjects well enough to support social research. Accurate, verifiable simulations could offer an accessible source of data about behavior and help train AI systems. The authors acknowledge that results so far have been limited and that adoption among social scientists remains low.

They ground their case in a review of comparisons between model-generated and human responses, commentary, and related research. Their position is that five tractable challenges can be addressed to realize the method's promise. Directions highlighted in the abstract include supplying richer context through prompts and fine-tuning models with social-science datasets.

The authors believe these simulations can already support pilot and exploratory studies, while broader use may become possible as capabilities advance. They recommend developing conceptual models and repeatedly evaluating simulations as systems change. This is a qualified research agenda: its promise depends on accuracy and verification, and the stated current use case is exploratory work rather than an established general replacement for human participants.
icml-2025-position-llm-social-simulation.tldr: The authors argue that validated LLM social simulations have promise, particularly for pilot and exploratory studies, if tractable challenges are addressed.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether medical language-model benchmarks actually measure the abilities claimed on their behalf. Strong results on licensing-exam questions often support statements about clinical knowledge or physician-like reasoning. The authors argue that such interpretations need empirical validation connecting benchmark performance to the real-world capability the benchmark is intended to represent.

They use the idea of construct validity from psychological testing. A construct is the underlying conceptual target of a test, and construct validity concerns whether the test measures that target. Drawing an analogy between psychological tests and language-model benchmarks provides a framework for investigating this relationship instead of assuming it from a benchmark's medical subject matter.

The authors conduct proof-of-concept experiments using real clinical data and report significant construct-validity gaps in popular medical benchmarks. They then propose an evaluation ecosystem centered on developing valid benchmarks. The findings challenge the interpretation of existing scores and support treating benchmark validation as an empirical task in its own right, alongside evaluating the models that take those tests.
icml-2025-position-medical-large-languag.tldr: The paper finds construct-validity gaps in popular medical LLM benchmarks and argues that their connection to intended clinical abilities should be tested empirically.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses a basic ambiguity in explainable machine learning: papers often introduce explanation algorithms without making their purpose or appropriate use sufficiently clear. The authors propose understanding explanations as statistics of high-dimensional functions. This connects explanation research to the practical questions that arise when interpreting more familiar statistical quantities.

Under this perspective, producing an explanation is only part of the task. Researchers also need to establish how the resulting quantity relates to the question a person actually wants to answer. A mathematical summary of a model and an intuitive question about the world do not establish that relationship by themselves; interpretation needs explicit attention.

The authors identify the limited discussion of this issue as a major weakness in the existing literature. Their contribution is a pragmatic conceptual framework for improving research practice through parallels with applied statistics. It redirects attention toward what explanations mean and how they should be used, giving researchers a basis for clarifying the purpose of an explanation method.
icml-2025-position-rethinking-explainabl.tldr: The authors propose treating model explanations as statistical quantities whose interpretation must be connected explicitly to the questions people want answered.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that organizing AI research around artificial general intelligence makes productive goal setting harder. The authors emphasize that the research community helps shape scientific, engineering, and societal priorities. Because AGI is highly contested, they question whether it can provide an effective shared direction for those different kinds of goals.

The paper identifies six traps aggravated by AGI discourse: Illusion of Consensus, Supercharging Bad Science, Presuming Value-Neutrality, Goal Lottery, Generality Debt, and Normalized Exclusion. These categories organize the authors' critique of how the overarching goal influences research priorities. Their concern is the quality of goal selection, including whose perspectives enter that process.

They propose three changes: state goals more specifically, recognize multiple worthwhile approaches and valuable outcomes, and include a broader range of disciplines and communities. Together, these recommendations replace reliance on a single contested destination with a more explicit and plural approach to research direction. The paper advances a position on how AI research should choose its goals, rather than reporting a technical route to AGI.
icml-2025-position-stop-treating-agi-as-.tldr: The authors argue that AI research should prioritize specific, plural, inclusive goals instead of treating contested AGI ambitions as its guiding objective.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that established consumer-protection laws can also support AI safety in the United States. The proposed mechanism is conditional: with appropriate enforcement and strengthening, these laws can give businesses incentives to build and deploy safer systems. The author presents existing legal protections as resources that already address unethical commercial behavior.

The argument responds to two positions in AI policy. One emphasizes entirely new AI-specific legislation, which the author considers valuable but difficult to draft and easy to evade. The other treats consumer protection as mere bureaucracy. Against that view, the paper points to existing laws that have already constrained some harmful business practices connected to AI.

The paper surveys consumer-protection laws and their effects on AI development and use, then calls for their enforcement and preservation amid deregulation. It also argues that the United States' litigation-oriented environment is well placed to support this approach. The contribution is a policy case for using and strengthening established institutions as part of AI safety, rather than assuming safety requires only new legislation.
icml-2025-position-strong-consumer-prote.tldr: The author argues that enforcing and strengthening existing U.S. consumer-protection laws can incentivize safer AI development and deployment.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the use of fixed racial categories in machine learning. Its central concern is that such categories embed assumptions about identity that do not travel reliably across societies. The authors describe prevailing taxonomies as centered on the United States and question their global applicability, highlighting Europe as a setting where race categories are not commonly used.

The critique also concerns what categorical representations leave out. Rigid groupings can oversimplify identity and erase mixed-race experiences. The authors argue that they can reinforce essentialist ideas about race that conflict with understanding race as socially constructed. The choice of categories therefore carries substantive assumptions about the people being represented.

The paper calls for research agendas that move beyond categorical variables when addressing discrimination and social inequality. Its contribution is a challenge to the framing of these problems, asking researchers to reconsider how racial identity is represented in the first place. The proposed direction keeps discrimination and inequality as research concerns while questioning whether fixed taxonomies adequately express them.
icml-2025-position-the-categorization-of.tldr: The paper critiques rigid, U.S.-centered racial categories in machine learning and calls for approaches beyond categorical variables to study discrimination.

paragraphs: RFRBoost constructs deep residual random-feature networks using boosting theory. At each layer, random features help learn a functional gradient of the network's representation: a direction for improving that representation. The method aims to gain the benefits of progressively improving a deep network while preserving the convex optimization advantages associated with random-feature models.

The optimization depends on the training loss. For mean squared error, the authors derive closed-form solutions for greedy layer-by-layer boosting. For general losses, fitting a random-feature residual block becomes a quadratically constrained least-squares problem. These results give the construction process an explicit optimization structure and connect the network's development to boosting-based theoretical guarantees.

Experiments cover tabular regression and classification in the small- to medium-scale setting where random-feature networks are typically used. The authors report significant improvements over random-feature networks and end-to-end trained multilayer-perceptron residual networks, together with substantial computational benefits. The demonstrated result is therefore scoped to this data regime, where representation boosting offers a promising combination of predictive performance and efficient optimization.
icml-2025-random-feature-representation-.tldr: RFRBoost builds residual random-feature networks layer by layer, improving tabular prediction while retaining structured, computationally efficient optimization.

paragraphs: SpikeVideoFormer extends spike-driven Transformers to video, where a model must process changes over time as well as spatial content. The authors argue that existing spiking Transformers concentrate mainly on individual images and therefore do not fully exploit spiking networks' efficiency for video tasks. Their design targets useful video representations with temporal complexity that grows linearly with sequence length.

The main component is spike-driven Hamming attention, presented as a theoretically guided adaptation of ordinary real-valued attention. The authors then analyze alternative ways to organize spike-driven attention across space and time. They identify a scheme that combines strong video-task performance with linear temporal complexity, making attention design central to the efficiency claim.

Evaluations cover video classification, human pose tracking, and semantic segmentation. The authors report state-of-the-art results among existing spiking approaches, including improvements exceeding 15% on tracking and segmentation. They also report matching recent conventional neural-network methods while achieving efficiency gains of 16, 10, and 5 times across the three respective tasks. These results support the architecture across several distinct video applications.
icml-2025-spikevideoformer-an-efficient-.tldr: SpikeVideoFormer uses spike-driven Hamming attention to achieve linear temporal complexity and strong results across three video tasks with reported efficiency gains.
